context_blurb:
On a sunny day, the warm light on your face comes from a star. The Sun is a giant ball of hot, glowing gas, and it sits at the centre of our solar system. Eight planets circle it, and Earth is one of them. The Sun's light and heat keep our world warm enough to live on.

The Sun is the nearest star to Earth. It outshines all the stars of the night sky because it is much closer to us than they are. Many stars are far bigger and hotter than the Sun. They are just so far away that they look like tiny points of light. A flashlight works the same way. Up close it lights a whole room, but far across a dark field it looks like a speck.

Why don't the planets fly off into space? The Sun's gravity, its pull, holds each planet on its path. Picture a ball on a string that you whirl around your head. The string pulls the ball toward your hand; let go, and the ball flies away. A planet is also racing forward all the time, so instead of falling into the Sun, it keeps curving around it. One trip all the way around the Sun takes Earth about 365 days, and that trip is what we call a year. A day is just one spin of Earth, and each of the four seasons lasts about three months.

Nearest the Sun are four small, rocky worlds. Mercury comes first, closest to the Sun of them all. Then come Venus, Earth and Mars. You might guess that Mercury, being so close, is the hottest planet, but it is not. It has almost no air, so its heat slips away into space. Venus is the hottest planet, because its thick air traps the heat like a heavy blanket. Its ground bakes at over 450 degrees Celsius, hot enough to melt lead. Bright clouds wrap Venus and help make it the brightest planet in the night sky.

Earth, the third planet, is our home. As far as anyone knows, Earth is the only planet with living things on it. It is also the only one known to have liquid water on its surface. Other planets share some of Earth's features. Every planet has gravity. Mars and the giant planets have moons, and clouds drift over Venus, Mars and Jupiter. Earth's gravity keeps our Moon travelling around us, about once a month. The Moon shines brightly at night, yet it makes no light of its own. The Moon reflects light from the Sun: moonlight is sunlight that bounces off its rocky ground and travels on to us. A bike reflector works the same way, glowing only when a light shines on it.

On a clear night, Mars, the fourth planet, shines like a reddish star. Mars is red because rusty dust covers its ground. Its rocks and dust are full of iron, and the iron has rusted, like an old nail left out in the rain. Red does not mean hot here. Mars is farther from the Sun than Earth is. Even on a warm day, its ground reaches only about 20 degrees Celsius, about room temperature.

Past Mars lies the asteroid belt, a ring of rocky chunks. Beyond it are four giant planets, great balls of gas and ice. Jupiter, the nearest giant, is the largest planet of all. It holds more than twice as much matter as all the other planets put together. Next comes Saturn. Every giant has rings, but Saturn's are the bright ones, made of countless chunks of ice and rock. The ice shines in sunlight, so Saturn's rings show up even in a small telescope. The other giants' rings are faint and dark. Beyond Saturn lie two ice giants, and the farther one, Neptune, is the most distant planet. Little Pluto, out past Neptune, is now called a dwarf planet.
